t.7.35.1: Then Rāma questioned the sage whose abode was in the southern quarter. With folded palms and full of humility, he spoke these meaningful words.
t.7.35.3: Valour, skill, strength, steadfastness, wisdom, the accomplishment of sound policy, prowess and power have all made their dwelling in Hanūmān.
t.7.35.2: Incomparable was the strength belonging to these two, Vālin and Rāvaṇa; yet neither of them was equal to Hanumān in prowess. Such is my opinion.
t.7.35.4: Then, seeing the ocean and the monkey host sinking into despair, he comforted the monkeys once more and leapt across a hundred yojanas.
t.7.35.5: Having assailed the city of Laṅkā and likewise the inner palace of Rāvaṇa, he saw Sītā, spoke with her, and likewise gave her reassurance.
t.7.35.6: The commanders at the head of the army, the sons of the ministers, the Kiṃkaras, and Rāvaṇa's son: all these were struck down there by Hanumān alone.
t.7.35.7: Then, freed from his bonds, after speaking with Daśānana, he reduced Laṅkā to ashes, as fire burns the earth.
t.7.35.8: Neither of Kāla, nor of Śakra, nor of Viṣṇu, nor of Vittapa are such deeds heard of as are those of Hanumat in battle.
t.7.35.9: By the might of this one's arms I have gained Laṅkā, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, and victory too, and my kingdom, my friends and my kinsmen.
t.7.35.10: If Hanūmān, the friend of the lord of the monkeys, were not mine, who would have been able to learn even the news of Jānakī?
t.7.35.11: And why, when the enmity arose back then, was Vālī not burned up by him like so many plants, out of his wish to do what was dear to Sugrīva?
t.7.35.12: For I think Hanumān did not know his own strength, since he looked on while the lord of the monkeys, dear to him as life itself, was suffering.
t.7.35.13: O blessed one, O great sage, honored by the immortals, tell me all this concerning Hanūmān in detail and as it truly is.
t.7.35.14: Having heard Rāghava's words, which were full of reason, the sage then spoke these words to him in the presence of Hanumān.
t.7.35.15: True is this, O best of the Raghus, which you say of Hanumān: there is none equal to him in strength, nor anyone superior to him in speed or in intellect.
t.7.35.16: But long ago a curse was laid upon him by the sages, whose curses never fail, and because of it this crusher of foes, though mighty, does not know his own strength.
t.7.35.17: O mighty Rāma, the deed that he performed even in his childhood cannot be described to you, so extremely young was he at the time.
t.7.35.18: But if, O Rāghava, you have the wish to hear it, then fix your mind on it, O Rāma, and listen as I tell it.
t.7.35.19: There is a mountain named Sumeru, made golden by a boon granted by Sūrya, where his father, named Kesarin, rules the kingdom.
t.7.35.20: His beloved wife was renowned by the name Añjanā. In her Vāyu begot an excellent son.
t.7.35.21: Then Añjanā gave birth to him, whose glow was like the golden ear of rice. Wishing to gather fruits, she went out, roaming in the dense forest.
t.7.35.22: Sorely afflicted by separation from his mother and by hunger, this child wept exceedingly, like the young king of the śarabhas.
t.7.35.24: Facing the rising sun, the child, like the young sun itself in bodily form, leapt through the midst of the sky, longing to seize the rising sun.
t.7.35.23: Then he saw the rising Vivasvant, resembling a heap of japā flowers, and out of greed for a fruit he leapt up toward Ravi.
t.7.35.25: As this Hanūmān, while still in his childhood, was leaping through the sky, a very great amazement arose among the Devas, Dānavas and Siddhas.
t.7.35.26: Neither the wind, nor Garuḍa, nor even the mind is as swift as this son of Vāyu as he strides across the highest sky.
t.7.35.27: If even now, while he is but a child, his speed and prowess are such as this, what will his swiftness be once he has attained youthful strength?
t.7.35.28: Vāyu followed close behind his own son as he leapt through the sky, guarding him from fear of being scorched by the sun, himself grown cool as a mass of snow.
t.7.35.29: Then he strode across the sky for many thousands of yojanas, and through his father's might and his own childishness he came near the sun.
t.7.35.30: Thinking, “This is but a child who knows no wrong, and a great task depends upon him,” the Sun, Divākara, did not burn him.
t.7.35.31: On the very day that this one leapt up to seize the sun, on that very day Rāhu was seeking to seize the maker of day.
t.7.35.32: And, O Rāma, seized by him atop the chariot of the Sun, Rāhu, the tormentor of the Moon and the Sun, fled from there in terror.
t.7.35.33: Having gone to the abode of Indra, the son of Siṃhikā, filled with wrath, knit his brows and spoke to the god, who was surrounded by hosts of deities.
t.7.35.34: O Vāsava, you gave me the moon and the sun to appease my hunger; why then, O slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, have you given this to another?
t.7.35.35: Today, at the time of the parvan, I came wishing to seize the sun, but then another Rāhu approached and suddenly seized the sun.
t.7.35.36: Having heard the words of Rāhu, Vāsava, filled with agitation, left his seat and sprang up, wearing his golden garland.
t.7.35.37: Then the four-tusked one, gleaming like a peak of Kailāsa, streaming with ichor, richly adorned and towering, its golden bells pealing like loud laughter—
t.7.35.38: Indra mounted the lord of elephants and, placing Rāhu in front, set out for the place where Sūrya was, together with this Hanūmān.
t.7.35.39: Then Rāhu, leaving Vāsava behind, went forth with great speed, and as he came rushing on like a mountain peak, he was indeed seen by this one.
t.7.35.40: Then, letting go of Sūrya and seeing Rāhu thus, he leapt up again into the sky to seize the son of Siṃhikā.
t.7.35.41: Seeing this monkey rushing toward him, Rāma, Rāhu, who is nothing but a head, let go of the sun, turned back and fled with his face averted.
t.7.35.42: But the son of Siṃhikā, looking to Indra as his protector, cried out again and again in terror, "Indra! Indra!"
t.7.35.43: Hearing the voice of Rāhu crying out, while he himself was still unseen, Indra said: “Do not be afraid; here I am, I will strike him down.”
t.7.35.44: Then, seeing Airāvata, Māruti thought, "This too is a great fruit," and rushed at that king of elephants.
t.7.35.45: Then, as he rushed on in his eagerness to seize Airāvata, his form became for a moment terrible and blazing, like that of Indra and Agni.
t.7.35.46: As he came rushing on in this way, Śacīpati, not greatly angered, struck him with the thunderbolt let fly from the tip of his hand.
t.7.35.47: Then, struck by Indra's thunderbolt, he fell upon the mountain, and as he was falling, his left jaw was broken.
t.7.35.48: But when that child had fallen, stricken and reeling from the blow of the thunderbolt, Pavana grew angry with Indra, and this boded ill for all creatures.
t.7.35.49: Entering into all creatures, the lord blocked the seat of excrement and urine, and so he obstructed all beings, just as Vāsava holds back the rains.
t.7.35.50: Through the wrath of Vāyu, living beings everywhere were left without breath; with their joints breaking, they became like pieces of wood.
t.7.35.51: Through the wrath of Vāyu, the three worlds, without svadhā and without vaṣaṭ, without rites and bereft of dharma, appeared as though fallen into hell.
t.7.35.52: Then the creatures, together with the Gandharvas, the Devas, the Asuras and humans, afflicted by suffering and longing for relief, ran together to Prajāpati.
t.7.35.53: The gods, their bellies like the hollow of a conch, spoke with joined palms: “O blessed one, O lord of creatures, it was by you that the four kinds of beings were created.”
t.7.35.54: This Pavana was given by you as the lord of our life. Having become the master of our breaths, why, O best of the virtuous, has he now turned against us?
t.7.35.55: Causing us suffering, he has shut us in, as women are confined in the inner apartments. Therefore, stricken by Vāyu, we have come to you for refuge, O lord.
t.7.35.56: O slayer of foes, dispel this suffering of ours that has arisen from the obstruction of the wind.
t.7.35.57: Having heard this from the creatures, Prajāpati, the lord of creatures, said to them, “It is for a reason,” and then spoke to the creatures again.
t.7.35.58: O creatures, hear all about the cause for which Vāyu grew angry with you and held you back. It ought to be heard, and it is fitting for one's own good.
t.7.35.59: His son has today been struck down by Indra, lord of the immortals. Heeding the words of Rāhu, the king has roused the Wind to anger against you.
t.7.35.60: Himself bodiless, Vāyu moves within bodies, sustaining them; for without Vāyu the body becomes no different from dust.
t.7.35.61: Vāyu is the life-breaths, Vāyu is happiness, Vāyu is this whole world. Abandoned by Vāyu, the world finds no happiness.
t.7.35.62: This very day the world has been abandoned by Vāyu, who is its very life; this very day these beings stand without breath, like logs of wood and walls.
t.7.35.63: Therefore let us go to where Māruta dwells, for it is he who has brought this affliction upon you; let us not meet destruction without first appeasing the son of Aditi.
t.7.35.64: Then Prajāpati, accompanied by the creatures and with the gods, Gandharvas, serpents and Guhyakas, went to the place where Māruta was, holding his son who had been struck down by the lord of the gods.
t.7.35.65: Then the Four-faced One, together with the gods, Siddhas, sages, serpents and Rākṣasas, beheld the son of Sadāgati, the ever-moving Wind, lying in his father's lap, radiant as the sun, as fire and as gold, and he was moved to compassion.
